glossary.definition: Substance that turns blue litmus red; produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution.
Substance that turns red litmus blue; produces OH⁻ ions in aqueous solution.
Substance that changes colour in acidic or basic medium (e.g. litmus).
Reaction of acid and base to form salt and water.
Measure of hydrogen ion concentration; 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 basic.
Ionic compound formed from acid-base reaction (or other neutralisation).
Fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a crystal.
Adding water to lower concentration; always add acid to water, slowly with stirring.

concepts.name: What are acids?
concepts.simple_answer: Acids are substances that taste sour, turn blue litmus red, and contain replaceable hydrogen.
concepts.why: Foundation of Ch 2 — acids introduced first.
concepts.example: Lemon juice and vinegar taste sour because of acids.
concepts.remember: Sour taste + blue litmus → red = acid clues.
concepts.common_confusion: Not all acids are safe to taste — lab acids are corrosive.

concepts.name: What are bases?
concepts.simple_answer: Bases are bitter, soapy to touch, turn red litmus blue, and include metal oxides/hydroxides.
concepts.example: Soap solution feels slippery — basic.
concepts.remember: Bitter + soapy feel + red litmus → blue = base.
concepts.common_confusion: Bases are not always solids — NaOH is aqueous base.

concepts.name: What are salts?
concepts.simple_answer: Salts are ionic compounds formed when acid reacts with base — e.g. NaCl, CuSO₄, Na₂CO₃.
concepts.example: Table salt NaCl from HCl + NaOH.
concepts.common_confusion: Not every salt comes from neutralisation — but most in Ch 2 do.

concepts.name: Natural sources of acids
concepts.simple_answer: Acids occur in fruits (citric), vinegar (acetic), curd (lactic), and stomach (HCl).
concepts.example: Tamarind and orange contain acids.
concepts.common_confusion: Natural acids are dilute; lab acids like conc. H₂SO₄ are dangerous.

concepts.name: Natural sources of bases
concepts.simple_answer: Bases include lime water Ca(OH)₂, baking soda NaHCO₃, and antacids like milk of magnesia Mg(OH)₂.
concepts.example: Whitewash uses slaked lime — basic.
concepts.remember: Lime, antacids, and soap are common bases.
concepts.common_confusion: Baking soda is hydrogencarbonate — amphoteric behaviour later.

concepts.name: Mineral acids vs organic acids
concepts.simple_answer: Mineral acids (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃) from minerals; organic acids (CH₃COOH, HCOOH) from living sources.

visual.formula: Mineral: HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃ | Organic: CH₃COOH

concepts.example: Vinegar contains acetic acid CH₃COOH.
concepts.common_confusion: Organic acids are generally weaker than mineral acids.

concepts.name: Strong vs weak acids (intro)
concepts.simple_answer: Strong acids ionise completely in water (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃); weak acids partially (CH₃COOH).
concepts.example: Dilute HCl conducts well — many ions.
concepts.common_confusion: Strength is not the same as concentration.

concepts.name: Alkalis
concepts.simple_answer: Water-soluble bases are called alkalis — NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂, NH₄OH dissolve to give OH⁻.
concepts.example: NaOH pellets dissolve in water — alkali.
concepts.remember: All alkalis are bases; not all bases are alkalis.
concepts.common_confusion: Mg(OH)₂ is a base but insoluble — not an alkali.

concepts.name: Indicators preview
concepts.simple_answer: Substances that change colour in acid or base — litmus, turmeric, methyl orange, phenolphthalein.
concepts.example: Blue litmus turns red in acid.
concepts.common_confusion: Universal indicator shows full pH range — Day 11.

concepts.name: Chapter 2 roadmap
concepts.simple_answer: Ch 2 covers acids, bases, salts, indicators, reactions, pH, everyday uses, and chemicals from common salt.
concepts.example: Activity 2.1–2.4 in lab sections.

concepts.name: What is an indicator?
concepts.simple_answer: An indicator is a substance that shows different colours in acidic and basic media.
concepts.example: Litmus paper distinguishes acid from base.
concepts.remember: One colour in acid, different in base.
concepts.common_confusion: Indicator does not measure exact pH unless universal indicator.

concepts.name: Litmus — source and colours
concepts.simple_answer: Litmus is a natural dye from lichen; turns red in acid, blue in base.

visual.formula: Acid: blue → red | Base: red → blue

concepts.example: Blue litmus paper dipped in HCl turns red.
concepts.remember: Blue litmus + acid → red; red litmus + base → blue.
concepts.common_confusion: Purple/neutral litmus in distilled water.

concepts.name: Red litmus in base
concepts.simple_answer: Red litmus paper turns blue in basic solution — confirms base.
concepts.example: NaOH solution turns red litmus blue.
concepts.common_confusion: Red litmus stays red in acid — no change.

concepts.name: Blue litmus in acid
concepts.simple_answer: Blue litmus paper turns red in acidic solution — confirms acid.
concepts.example: Dilute HCl turns blue litmus red.
concepts.common_confusion: Blue litmus stays blue in base.

concepts.name: Turmeric as indicator
concepts.simple_answer: Turmeric (haldi) is natural indicator — yellow in neutral/acid, reddish-brown in base.
concepts.example: Soap on turmeric stain turns red-brown.
concepts.remember: Turmeric paper detects base at home.
concepts.common_confusion: Turmeric does not change in acid — stays yellow.

concepts.name: China rose (Gudhal) indicator
concepts.simple_answer: China rose petal extract: dark pink in acid, green in base.
concepts.example: Petals soaked in hot water give extract.
concepts.common_confusion: Not as common as litmus in exams.

concepts.name: Methyl orange
concepts.simple_answer: Synthetic indicator methyl orange: red in strong acid, yellow in strong base, orange in neutral.
concepts.example: Used in titration to mark end point.
concepts.remember: Red in acid; yellow in base.
concepts.common_confusion: Orange in near-neutral pH.

concepts.name: Phenolphthalein
concepts.simple_answer: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid, pink/fuchsia in base.
concepts.example: NaOH turns phenolphthalein pink.
concepts.remember: Colourless in acid; pink in base.
concepts.common_confusion: Very faint pink near pH 8 — endpoint in titration.

concepts.name: Natural vs synthetic indicators
concepts.simple_answer: Natural: litmus, turmeric, china rose. Synthetic: methyl orange, phenolphthalein.
concepts.example: Litmus from lichen — natural.
concepts.remember: Natural from plants; synthetic made in lab.
concepts.common_confusion: Both work on same principle — colour change.

concepts.name: Choosing an indicator
concepts.simple_answer: Pick indicator whose colour change matches expected pH range of titration or test.
concepts.example: Phenolphthalein for strong acid–strong base titration.
concepts.remember: Indicator must change in range of reaction.
concepts.common_confusion: Wrong indicator may miss endpoint.

days.title: Acids and Bases in the Laboratory (Activity 2.1)

concepts.name: Activity 2.1 — acids in lab
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 2.1: collect samples of HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃, CH₃COOH, NaOH, Ca(OH)₂, KOH, Mg(OH)₂, NH₄OH.
concepts.example: Test each with litmus and indicators.
concepts.common_confusion: Handle acids and bases with care — corrosive.

concepts.name: Hydrochloric acid HCl
concepts.simple_answer: HCl is a strong mineral acid — colourless, pungent, turns blue litmus red.
concepts.example: Present in stomach for digestion.
concepts.remember: Strong acid; fully ionises in water.
concepts.common_confusion: Never called hydrochloric acid(HCl) without 'acid'.

concepts.name: Sulphuric acid H₂SO₄
concepts.simple_answer: H₂SO₄ is strong mineral acid — dense, oily, dibasic acid used in industry.
concepts.example: Car batteries contain dilute H₂SO₄.
concepts.common_confusion: Concentrated H₂SO₄ is highly corrosive — add to water only.

concepts.name: Nitric acid HNO₃
concepts.simple_answer: HNO₃ is strong mineral acid — used in fertilisers and explosives manufacture.
concepts.example: Reacts with metals; often gives NO₂ with copper.
concepts.remember: Strong acid; oxidising nature with metals.
concepts.common_confusion: Not all metal + HNO₃ give H₂ — oxidising acid.

concepts.name: Acetic acid CH₃COOH
concepts.simple_answer: CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid) is weak organic acid in vinegar (~4–5%).
concepts.example: Vinegar for cooking and pickling.
concepts.common_confusion: Vinegar is dilute acetic acid, not HCl.

concepts.name: Sodium hydroxide NaOH
concepts.simple_answer: NaOH (caustic soda) is strong alkali — white pellets, corrosive, turns red litmus blue.
concepts.example: Used in soap and paper industry.
concepts.common_confusion: Caustic — never touch with wet hands.

concepts.name: Calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)₂
concepts.simple_answer: Ca(OH)₂ (slaked lime) is alkali — used in whitewash and water treatment.
concepts.example: Turns milky with CO₂ — test for carbon dioxide.
concepts.remember: Less soluble than NaOH but still alkali.
concepts.common_confusion: Limewater = Ca(OH)₂ aqueous, not CaO.

concepts.name: Potassium hydroxide KOH
concepts.simple_answer: KOH (caustic potash) is strong alkali — similar to NaOH, used in soft soaps.
concepts.example: Soft soap from KOH + fat.
concepts.common_confusion: KOH and NaOH both strong — do not taste either.

concepts.name: Magnesium hydroxide Mg(OH)₂
concepts.simple_answer: Mg(OH)₂ (milk of magnesia) is weakly soluble base — antacid for indigestion.
concepts.example: Neutralises excess stomach HCl.
concepts.common_confusion: Milk of magnesia is suspension, not clear solution.

concepts.name: Ammonium hydroxide NH₄OH
concepts.simple_answer: NH₄OH (ammonia solution) is weak alkali — pungent smell, cleaning agent.
concepts.example: Window cleaner contains ammonia.
concepts.common_confusion: Formula NH₄OH represents aqueous ammonia.

concepts.name: Acid + metal reaction (general)
concepts.simple_answer: Acid reacts with metal to give salt and hydrogen gas.
concepts.example: Zn + HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.
concepts.common_confusion: Only metals above H in reactivity series with dilute acid.

concepts.name: Zinc and dilute HCl
concepts.simple_answer: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ — bubbles of hydrogen, zinc dissolves.
concepts.example: Activity from Ch 1 revisited in Ch 2 context.
concepts.common_confusion: Copper does not react with dilute HCl.

concepts.name: Magnesium and dilute H₂SO₄
concepts.simple_answer: Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂ — vigorous reaction, hydrogen evolved.
concepts.example: Mg ribbon reacts faster than Zn.
concepts.common_confusion: Hot and fast — handle with tongs.

concepts.name: Iron and dilute acid
concepts.simple_answer: Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂ — iron nails produce hydrogen slowly.
concepts.example: Pale green FeCl₂ solution forms.
concepts.remember: Iron displaces H from dilute acid.
concepts.common_confusion: Fe with conc. HNO₃ may not give H₂ — passivation.

concepts.name: Testing for hydrogen gas
concepts.simple_answer: Bring burning splint to mouth of tube — hydrogen burns with pop sound.
concepts.example: Activity 2.2 hydrogen test.
concepts.common_confusion: Oxygen relights splint — do not confuse.

concepts.name: Why hydrogen forms
concepts.simple_answer: Acids contain replaceable H⁺; reactive metal displaces H as H₂ gas.
concepts.example: Zn loses electrons; H⁺ gains to form H₂.
concepts.common_confusion: Unreactive metals (Cu, Ag, Au) no reaction.

concepts.name: Reactivity series restriction
concepts.simple_answer: Only metals above hydrogen in reactivity series react with dilute acids to give H₂.
concepts.example: Mg, Zn, Fe react; Cu does not.
concepts.common_confusion: Series order: Mg > Zn > Fe > H > Cu.

concepts.name: Salt name from acid
concepts.simple_answer: From HCl → chloride salt; H₂SO₄ → sulphate; HNO₃ → nitrate; CH₃COOH → acetate.
concepts.example: Zn + HCl → zinc chloride.
concepts.remember: Anion from acid names the salt.
concepts.common_confusion: Sulphuric acid always gives sulphate salts.

concepts.name: Safety with acid-metal reactions
concepts.simple_answer: Use dilute acid, small metal pieces, test tube tilted, never add water to acid.
concepts.example: Wear goggles; hydrogen is flammable.
concepts.remember: Dilute acid + small pieces + splint test.
concepts.common_confusion: Never look directly into mouth of tube when testing gas.

concepts.name: Exam pattern — acid and metal
concepts.simple_answer: Typical question: write equation, name salt, describe H₂ test with pop sound.
concepts.example: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂; pop with splint.
concepts.common_confusion: Balance equation for full marks.

concepts.name: Acid + carbonate (general)
concepts.simple_answer: Acid reacts with metal carbonate to give salt, water, and carbon dioxide.
concepts.example: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂.
concepts.common_confusion: Three products — not same as acid + metal.

concepts.name: Acid + hydrogencarbonate
concepts.simple_answer: Acid reacts with hydrogencarbonate (bicarbonate) to give salt, water, and CO₂.
concepts.example: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
concepts.common_confusion: Hydrogencarbonate also releases CO₂.
concepts.optional_detail: NaHCO₃ is baking soda — Ch 2 later section.

concepts.name: Marble and dilute HCl
concepts.simple_answer: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ — marble effervesces.
concepts.example: Chalk and marble both contain CaCO₃.
concepts.common_confusion: Marble is CaCO₃ — same as limestone.

concepts.name: Sodium carbonate and acid
concepts.simple_answer: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ — washing soda reacts with acid.
concepts.example: CO₂ turns lime water milky.
concepts.common_confusion: Na₂CO₃ is washing soda (anhydrous form later).

concepts.name: Baking soda and vinegar
concepts.simple_answer: NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂ — kitchen reaction.
concepts.example: Cake rises from CO₂ in batter.
concepts.common_confusion: This CO₂ leavens bread and cakes.

concepts.name: Testing for carbon dioxide
concepts.simple_answer: Pass CO₂ through lime water Ca(OH)₂ — turns milky due to CaCO₃ precipitate.
concepts.example: Activity 2.2 CO₂ test.
concepts.common_confusion: Excess CO₂ clears milkiness — Ca(HCO₃)₂ forms.

concepts.name: Why CO₂ forms with carbonate
concepts.simple_answer: H⁺ from acid reacts with CO₃²⁻ or HCO₃⁻ to release H₂CO₃ which decomposes to H₂O + CO₂.
concepts.example: Effervescence is CO₂ escaping.
concepts.remember: Carbonate ion breaks down to CO₂ in acid.
concepts.common_confusion: Same test (milky lime water) for all carbonate/acid reactions.

concepts.name: Compare acid+metal vs acid+carbonate
concepts.simple_answer: Acid + metal → salt + H₂. Acid + carbonate → salt + H₂O + CO₂.
concepts.example: Pop test for H₂; milky lime water for CO₂.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not confuse H₂ pop with CO₂ milky test.

concepts.name: Activity 2.2 context
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 2.2: react acids with metal carbonates/hydrogencarbonates; test CO₂ with lime water.
concepts.example: NaHCO₃ + HCl in test tube → bubble through limewater.
concepts.common_confusion: Activity also includes acid + metal for H₂.

concepts.name: Exam template — acid and carbonate
concepts.simple_answer: Write balanced equation + state CO₂ test (lime water turns milky) + name all products.
concepts.example: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; milky limewater.
concepts.common_confusion: Include H₂O as product — often forgotten.

concepts.name: Neutralisation definition
concepts.simple_answer: Neutralisation is reaction between acid and base to form salt and water.
concepts.example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
concepts.remember: Acid + base cancel each other's effects.
concepts.common_confusion: Also a double displacement reaction.

concepts.name: NaOH and HCl
concepts.simple_answer: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O — classic strong acid–strong base neutralisation.
concepts.example: Antacid neutralises stomach acid similarly.
concepts.common_confusion: Needs balancing: coefficients are 1:1:1:1.

concepts.name: H₂SO₄ and KOH
concepts.simple_answer: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O — dibasic acid needs two moles of base.
concepts.example: Two OH⁻ needed per H₂SO₄.
concepts.common_confusion: H₂SO₄ has two replaceable H.

concepts.name: Ca(OH)₂ and HCl
concepts.simple_answer: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O — lime neutralises acid.
concepts.example: Farmers add lime to neutralise acidic soil.
concepts.remember: Two HCl per Ca(OH)₂ — two OH⁻.

concepts.name: NH₄OH and HNO₃
concepts.simple_answer: NH₄OH + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃ + H₂O — ammonium nitrate salt formed.
concepts.example: Fertiliser ammonium nitrate from this salt.
concepts.common_confusion: NH₄NO₃ is important fertiliser salt.

concepts.name: Neutralisation is exothermic
concepts.simple_answer: Neutralisation releases heat — test tube feels warm when acid and base mix.
concepts.example: Hand on mixed NaOH + HCl feels warm.
concepts.common_confusion: Not all students feel heat with dilute solutions.

concepts.name: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
concepts.simple_answer: At ionic level: hydrogen ion from acid combines with hydroxide from base to form water.
concepts.example: Net ionic equation for all strong acid–strong base.
concepts.common_confusion: Salt ions remain in solution (spectator ions).

concepts.name: Uses of neutralisation
concepts.simple_answer: Antacids for indigestion, treating acidic soil with lime, factory waste treatment.
concepts.example: Mg(OH)₂ neutralises excess HCl in stomach.
concepts.remember: Base added to excess acid (or vice versa).
concepts.common_confusion: Wasps sting basic — vinegar (acid) relieves.

concepts.name: Activity 2.3 — neutralisation
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 2.3: warm test tube when acid and base mixed — exothermic neutralisation.
concepts.example: NaOH + HCl in test tube — feel warmth.
concepts.common_confusion: Compare before mixing vs after.

concepts.name: Exam template — neutralisation
concepts.simple_answer: Define neutralisation → general equation → specific example → note exothermic + H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
concepts.example: 5-mark: definition + equation + application + exothermic.
concepts.common_confusion: Always balance the equation.

concepts.name: Metallic oxides are basic
concepts.simple_answer: Oxides of metals are generally basic — turn red litmus blue, react with acids.
concepts.example: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O.
concepts.common_confusion: Basic oxide reacts like a base with acid.

concepts.name: Copper oxide and sulphuric acid
concepts.simple_answer: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O — black CuO dissolves, blue solution forms.
concepts.example: Blue CuSO₄ solution after reaction.
concepts.common_confusion: Same pattern as neutralisation.

concepts.name: Calcium oxide and HCl
concepts.simple_answer: CaO + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O — quick lime reacts with acid.
concepts.example: Neutralises acid in industrial waste.

concepts.name: Magnesium oxide and acid
concepts.simple_answer: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O — magnesium oxide neutralises acid.
concepts.example: White MgO ash from Activity 1.1 is basic.
concepts.remember: Metal oxide from burning Mg reacts with acid.
concepts.common_confusion: MgO dissolves in acid — ash is not inert.

concepts.name: Iron(III) oxide and acid
concepts.simple_answer: Fe₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2FeCl₃ + 3H₂O — rust component reacts with acid.
concepts.example: Acid removes rust from iron — but also attacks iron.
concepts.common_confusion: Fe₂O₃ is basic oxide of iron.

concepts.name: Why metal oxides are basic
concepts.simple_answer: Metal oxides contain O²⁻ that accepts H⁺ from acid — behave like bases.
concepts.example: Na₂O, CaO, CuO all react with acids.
concepts.common_confusion: Not all metal oxides — Al₂O₃ is amphoteric (advanced).

concepts.name: Basic oxide + acid = neutralisation
concepts.simple_answer: Reaction of basic metal oxide with acid is a type of neutralisation — salt and water formed.
concepts.example: CuO + H₂SO₄ same product pattern as Cu(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄.
concepts.common_confusion: No H₂ or CO₂ from oxide + acid.

concepts.name: Activity 2.4 — metal oxides
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 2.4: react copper oxide with dilute H₂SO₄ — blue solution proves basic oxide.
concepts.example: Black solid dissolves → blue CuSO₄.
concepts.common_confusion: Heat may be needed to start CuO reaction.

concepts.name: Compare metal oxide vs metal with acid
concepts.simple_answer: Metal + acid → salt + H₂. Metal oxide + acid → salt + H₂O (no gas).
concepts.example: CuO + H₂SO₄ gives no gas; Zn + H₂SO₄ gives H₂.
concepts.common_confusion: No pop test for oxide + acid.

concepts.name: Exam — metallic oxides and acids
concepts.simple_answer: State metal oxides are basic → give general equation → CuO + H₂SO₄ example → link to neutralisation.
concepts.example: Basic oxide + acid → salt + water.
concepts.common_confusion: Name salt correctly: CuSO₄ = copper sulphate.

concepts.name: Non-metallic oxides are acidic
concepts.simple_answer: Oxides of non-metals are generally acidic — dissolve in water to form acids; react with bases.
concepts.example: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O.
concepts.common_confusion: Opposite of basic metal oxides.

concepts.name: Carbon dioxide and lime water
concepts.simple_answer: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O — lime water turns milky (also CO₂ test).
concepts.example: Used to test CO₂ from carbonate + acid.
concepts.common_confusion: Same equation as CO₂ test — dual purpose.

concepts.name: Carbon dioxide and sodium hydroxide
concepts.simple_answer: CO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O — CO₂ absorbed by caustic soda.
concepts.example: NaOH absorbs CO₂ in labs.
concepts.common_confusion: Na₂CO₃ is washing soda family.

concepts.name: Sulphur dioxide and NaOH
concepts.simple_answer: SO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₃ + H₂O — sulphur dioxide is acidic oxide.
concepts.example: SO₂ from burning sulphur-containing fuel.
concepts.common_confusion: SO₂ causes acid rain when dissolved in rain.

concepts.name: SO₂ and lime water
concepts.simple_answer: SO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaSO₃ + H₂O — similar to CO₂ but different salt.
concepts.example: Acid rain neutralised by limestone.
concepts.common_confusion: CaSO₃ not milky like CaCO₃ — different test.

concepts.name: Acidic oxide + water
concepts.simple_answer: Many non-metal oxides form acids in water: CO₂ → carbonic acid; SO₂ → sulphurous acid.

visual.note: Acidic oxide forms acid in water

concepts.why: Why they are called acidic oxides.
concepts.example: Rain dissolves CO₂ — slightly acidic rain.
concepts.common_confusion: H₂CO₃ is weak acid — carbonated water.

concepts.name: Compare metal vs non-metal oxides
concepts.simple_answer: Metal oxides basic (react with acid); non-metal oxides acidic (react with base).

visual.formula: Metal oxide + Acid | Non-metal oxide + Base

concepts.example: CuO + H₂SO₄ vs CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂.
concepts.remember: Basic vs acidic oxides — opposite partners.
concepts.common_confusion: Amphoteric oxides (Al₂O₃) are exception.

concepts.name: Acid rain connection
concepts.simple_answer: SO₂ and NO₂ (non-metal oxides) dissolve in rain forming acids — acid rain damages buildings and plants.
concepts.example: Taj Mahal affected by acid rain.
concepts.common_confusion: Limestone neutralises acid rain on statues.

concepts.name: Sulphur trioxide and water
concepts.simple_answer: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ — sulphur trioxide forms sulphuric acid in water.
concepts.example: Industrial contact process step.
concepts.common_confusion: SO₃ is dangerous — reacts violently with water.

concepts.name: Exam — non-metallic oxides and bases
concepts.simple_answer: State non-metal oxides are acidic → CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ equation → milky test → compare with basic metal oxides.
concepts.example: Mirror answer to Day 7 metal oxides.
concepts.common_confusion: Identify acidic vs basic oxide from metal/non-metal.

days.title: What Acids and Bases Have in Common

concepts.name: Common feature — H⁺ in acids
concepts.simple_answer: All acids produce hydrogen ions H⁺ (or hydronium H₃O⁺) in aqueous solution.

visual.note: H⁺ is common to all acids

concepts.example: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ in water.
concepts.remember: Acids characterised by H⁺ in water.
concepts.common_confusion: Dry acids (no water) do not show acidic properties.

concepts.name: Common feature — OH⁻ in bases
concepts.simple_answer: All bases produce hydroxide ions OH⁻ in aqueous solution (or accept H⁺).

visual.note: OH⁻ is common to all bases

concepts.example: NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻ in water.
concepts.remember: Bases characterised by OH⁻ in water.
concepts.common_confusion: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ — ammonia accepts H⁺ from water.

concepts.name: Acids need water to show acidity
concepts.simple_answer: Dry HCl gas does not turn blue litmus red — water needed to ionise and produce H⁺.
concepts.example: HCl gas over dry litmus — no change.
concepts.remember: No water → no H⁺ → no acid behaviour.
concepts.common_confusion: Acidic properties in aqueous solution only.

concepts.name: Bases need water for alkalinity
concepts.simple_answer: NaOH solid must dissolve in water to produce OH⁻ and show basic properties.
concepts.example: NaOH pellets in water → red litmus blue.
concepts.common_confusion: Dry base may not affect dry litmus.

concepts.name: Hydronium ion H₃O⁺
concepts.simple_answer: In water, H⁺ attaches to H₂O forming hydronium ion H₃O⁺ — actual species in solution.
concepts.example: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.
concepts.remember: H₃O⁺ is H⁺ in aqueous acid.
concepts.common_confusion: Textbook often writes H⁺ for simplicity.

concepts.name: Ionisation of acids
concepts.simple_answer: Strong acids ionise completely; weak acids partially in water.
concepts.example: Conductivity test: strong acid conducts better.
concepts.common_confusion: Ionisation degree differs; both produce H⁺.

concepts.name: Ionisation of bases
concepts.simple_answer: Strong bases (NaOH, KOH) ionise completely; weak bases (NH₄OH) partially.
concepts.example: Ca(OH)₂ sparingly soluble — limited OH⁻.
concepts.remember: More OH⁻ = stronger base in water.
concepts.common_confusion: Insoluble bases release few OH⁻ ions.

concepts.name: Electrical conductivity
concepts.simple_answer: Acid and base solutions conduct electricity due to ions H⁺/OH⁻ — electrolytes.
concepts.example: Bulb glows in HCl and NaOH solutions.
concepts.common_confusion: Pure water has very few ions — poor conductor.

concepts.name: What acids and bases have in common — summary
concepts.simple_answer: Both are electrolytes in water; acids give H⁺, bases give OH⁻; both react to neutralise each other.

visual.formula: Acid: H⁺ | Base: OH⁻ | Together: H₂O

concepts.example: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O in every neutralisation.
concepts.remember: Ions in water explain all Ch 2 behaviour.
concepts.common_confusion: Dry state ≠ aqueous behaviour.

concepts.name: Exam — common features
concepts.simple_answer: Explain acids produce H⁺ and bases OH⁻ in water; water required; give HCl and NaOH examples.

visual.label: Exam: H⁺ and OH⁻ common features

concepts.example: Dry HCl no effect on litmus — key point.
concepts.remember: State need for water + ion equations.
concepts.common_confusion: Distinguish strength from presence of H⁺.

days.title: Acids and Bases in Water — Ions and Dilution

concepts.name: Acids in water — ion formation
concepts.simple_answer: When acid dissolves in water, it releases H⁺ ions — responsible for all acidic properties.
concepts.example: H₂SO₄ → 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ in water.
concepts.common_confusion: Without water, no ionisation.

concepts.name: Bases in water — OH⁻ formation
concepts.simple_answer: When base dissolves in water, it releases OH⁻ ions — responsible for basic properties.
concepts.example: KOH → K⁺ + OH⁻.
concepts.common_confusion: NH₃ uses water to produce OH⁻ indirectly.

concepts.name: Dilution of acids
concepts.simple_answer: Dilution means adding water to make acid less concentrated — always add acid to water, never reverse.
concepts.example: Conc. H₂SO₄ + water safely: acid poured into water.
concepts.common_confusion: Water to conc. acid causes violent splashing — burns.

concepts.name: Why add acid to water
concepts.simple_answer: Dilution is exothermic; adding acid to large volume of water absorbs heat safely.
concepts.example: Conc. H₂SO₄ dilution can boil and spatter.
concepts.common_confusion: Always use glass rod stirring while adding acid.

concepts.name: Concentrated vs dilute acid
concepts.simple_answer: Concentrated = more acid particles per volume; dilute = more water — both can be strong acids.
concepts.example: Conc. HCl and dilute HCl both strong — differ in concentration.
concepts.common_confusion: Strength = ionisation; concentration = amount dissolved.

concepts.name: Dilution and ion concentration
concepts.simple_answer: Diluting acid reduces H⁺ concentration per unit volume — less corrosive but still acidic.
concepts.example: Dilute HCl safer for lab metal reactions.
concepts.remember: More water → fewer H⁺ per mL.
concepts.common_confusion: Dilute acid still turns blue litmus red.

concepts.name: Strong acid dilution
concepts.simple_answer: Even dilute strong acid fully ionised — every molecule gives H⁺, just fewer molecules present.

visual.formula: Dilute HCl: still H⁺ + Cl⁻ fully

concepts.example: 0.1 M HCl still strong acid.
concepts.common_confusion: Weak acid stays weak when diluted.

concepts.name: Indicators and dilution
concepts.simple_answer: Dilute acid still turns blue litmus red — indicator detects H⁺ presence not concentration alone.
concepts.example: Very dilute HCl still red litmus.
concepts.remember: Any H⁺ present → acidic to indicator.
concepts.common_confusion: Universal indicator colour may shift with concentration.

concepts.name: Preparing dilute HCl in lab
concepts.simple_answer: Add concentrated HCl slowly to water in beaker, stir with glass rod, wear goggles and lab coat.
concepts.example: Small volume acid into large volume water.
concepts.common_confusion: Work in fume cupboard for volatile acids.

concepts.name: Exam — dilution and ions
concepts.simple_answer: Explain H⁺/OH⁻ in water; dilution definition; acid-to-water rule; distinguish concentration from strength.
concepts.example: Never add water to conc. H₂SO₄ — safety mark.
concepts.remember: Four concepts in one long answer.
concepts.common_confusion: Include exothermic dilution note.

days.title: pH Scale and Strength of Acids/Bases

concepts.name: pH scale definition
concepts.simple_answer: pH scale measures acidity or alkalinity from 0 to 14 — pH 7 neutral, below 7 acid, above 7 base.
concepts.example: Pure water pH 7 at 25°C.
concepts.remember: Lower pH = more acidic; higher = more basic.
concepts.common_confusion: pH is logarithmic scale — each unit is 10× change.

concepts.name: pH of acids
concepts.simple_answer: Acids have pH less than 7 — stronger acids have lower pH (closer to 0).
concepts.example: Stomach acid pH ~1–2.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not say pH 0 for all strong acids in school lab.

concepts.name: pH of bases
concepts.simple_answer: Bases have pH greater than 7 — stronger bases have higher pH (closer to 14).
concepts.example: NaOH solution pH ~14.
concepts.common_confusion: Mild bases pH 8–10; strong bases 12–14.

concepts.name: Universal indicator
concepts.simple_answer: Universal indicator is mixture showing different colours across pH 0–14 — full spectrum.
concepts.example: Green at pH 7; red in strong acid; purple in strong base.
concepts.remember: One indicator for entire pH range.
concepts.common_confusion: Different from litmus which is red/blue only.

concepts.name: pH paper
concepts.simple_answer: pH paper dipped in solution gives colour matched to chart for approximate pH value.
concepts.example: Compare wet paper colour to standard chart.
concepts.common_confusion: Less precise than pH meter.

concepts.name: Strength vs pH
concepts.simple_answer: Stronger acid has lower pH at same concentration; stronger base has higher pH.

visual.formula: Strong HCl pH < weak CH₃COOH pH

concepts.example: 0.1 M HCl pH ~1; 0.1 M CH₃COOH pH ~3.
concepts.common_confusion: Concentration also affects pH — control variables.

concepts.name: Neutral pH 7
concepts.simple_answer: pH 7 is neutral — equal H⁺ and OH⁻; pure water and salt solutions may be neutral.
concepts.example: Distilled water pH 7 (at 25°C).
concepts.common_confusion: Rain water pH slightly below 7 due to dissolved CO₂.

concepts.name: pH and H⁺ concentration
concepts.simple_answer: Lower pH means higher H⁺ concentration — pH measures hydrogen ion concentration.
concepts.example: pH 3 has more H⁺ than pH 5.
concepts.common_confusion: Formula pH = -log[H⁺] — beyond Class 10 scope.

concepts.name: Mixing acid and base — pH change
concepts.simple_answer: Adding base to acid raises pH toward 7; adding acid to base lowers pH toward 7.
concepts.example: Excess NaOH added to HCl → pH rises above 7.
concepts.common_confusion: At exact equivalence, strong acid + strong base → pH 7.

concepts.name: Exam — pH scale
concepts.simple_answer: Define pH scale 0–14; pH 7 neutral; universal indicator; compare strong vs weak acid pH.
concepts.example: Include stomach pH ~2 as example.
concepts.common_confusion: State acid < 7, base > 7 clearly.

days.title: Importance of pH in Everyday Life

concepts.name: pH in soil
concepts.simple_answer: Plants need specific soil pH; acidic soil treated with lime Ca(OH)₂; basic soil with organic matter.
concepts.example: Tea coffee grow in acidic soil; cabbage in neutral.
concepts.remember: Farmer adjusts soil pH for crop.
concepts.common_confusion: Litmus can test soil solution pH roughly.

concepts.name: pH in stomach
concepts.simple_answer: Stomach produces HCl pH ~1–2 for digestion; excess acid causes indigestion — treated with antacids.
concepts.example: Mg(OH)₂ or NaHCO₃ neutralises excess acid.
concepts.common_confusion: Antacid does not stop normal digestion permanently.

concepts.name: pH in mouth
concepts.simple_answer: Tooth decay starts when mouth pH drops below 5.5 — bacteria produce acids from food.
concepts.example: Sugary food → acid → cavity.
concepts.common_confusion: Toothpaste is basic — neutralises mouth acid.

concepts.name: Bee sting vs wasp sting
concepts.simple_answer: Bee sting acidic (formic acid) — treat with baking soda (base); wasp sting basic — treat with vinegar (acid).

visual.formula: Bee: acid → base | Wasp: base → acid

concepts.example: Baking soda paste on bee sting.
concepts.common_confusion: Both stings painful — wrong treatment won't help.

concepts.name: Self-defence by animals
concepts.simple_answer: Ants and bees inject acid; stingray and many insects inject base — neutralisation explains treatment.
concepts.example: Nettle hair injects methanoic acid — dock leaf base relieves.
concepts.remember: Know sting type → choose acid or base remedy.
concepts.common_confusion: Not all insect bites are acid — identify first.

concepts.name: pH of river water
concepts.simple_answer: Living organisms sensitive to pH; factory waste can change river pH and kill fish.
concepts.example: Acidic factory effluent lowers river pH.
concepts.remember: Monitor pH to protect aquatic life.
concepts.common_confusion: Neutralise waste before discharge.

concepts.name: pH in food preservation
concepts.simple_answer: pH affects bacteria growth; acidic foods (pickles, citrus) preserve better.
concepts.example: Pickle in vinegar — low pH prevents spoilage.
concepts.common_confusion: Not all preservation is pH alone — also salt and sugar.

concepts.name: Hydrangea flower colour
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT mentions soil pH affects flower colour — acidic soil blue flowers, basic soil pink.
concepts.example: Gardeners adjust soil pH for colour.
concepts.common_confusion: Memorable exam example.

concepts.name: Measuring pH at home
concepts.simple_answer: Litmus, turmeric, universal indicator paper can estimate pH of soil, water, and food samples.
concepts.example: Turmeric on soap — red-brown confirms base.
concepts.common_confusion: pH meter most accurate — not home usual.

concepts.name: Exam — pH in everyday life
concepts.simple_answer: Give three examples: soil pH + lime, stomach + antacid, bee/wasp sting + treatment; explain each.
concepts.example: Three NCERT examples minimum for full marks.
concepts.common_confusion: Bee vs wasp opposite treatment — favourite exam trap.

days.title: Salts — Introduction and Family of Salts

concepts.name: What is a salt?
concepts.simple_answer: Salt is ionic compound formed from acid-base reaction, named by cation + anion — NaCl, ZnSO₄, CuSO₄.
concepts.example: NaCl from HCl + NaOH.
concepts.common_confusion: Salts can be acidic, basic, or neutral — Day 14.

concepts.name: Family of salts — NaCl
concepts.simple_answer: Sodium chloride NaCl from HCl + NaOH — table salt, essential for life and industry.
concepts.example: Preservation and seasoning.
concepts.remember: Chloride from HCl; sodium from NaOH.
concepts.common_confusion: NaCl source for chlor-alkali industry — Day 15.

concepts.name: Zinc sulphate ZnSO₄
concepts.simple_answer: ZnSO₄ from H₂SO₄ + Zn or ZnO + H₂SO₄ — white crystals used in medicine and agriculture.
concepts.example: Zinc sulphate eye drops.
concepts.common_confusion: Same salt from metal or basic oxide route.

concepts.name: Copper sulphate CuSO₄
concepts.simple_answer: CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue vitriol — from CuO + H₂SO₄; used in agriculture and electroplating.
concepts.example: Fungicide in farming.
concepts.common_confusion: Water of crystallisation — Day 16.

concepts.name: Sodium sulphate Na₂SO₄
concepts.simple_answer: Na₂SO₄ from H₂SO₄ + Na₂CO₃ or NaOH — white solid, detergent industry.
concepts.example: By-product of chemical industry.
concepts.common_confusion: Different from sodium sulphite Na₂SO₃.

concepts.name: Calcium chloride CaCl₂
concepts.simple_answer: CaCl₂ from HCl + CaCO₃ or CaO + HCl — de-icing roads, drying agent.
concepts.example: Hygroscopic — absorbs moisture.
concepts.common_confusion: Used to melt ice on roads.

concepts.name: Potassium nitrate KNO₃
concepts.simple_answer: KNO₃ from HNO₃ + KOH — fertiliser and gunpowder component.
concepts.example: Nitrate fertiliser for plants.
concepts.common_confusion: Also called saltpetre historically.

concepts.name: Naming salts
concepts.simple_answer: Salt name: metal/non-metal cation + acid radical — chloride, sulphate, nitrate, acetate.

visual.formula: HCl → chloride | H₂SO₄ → sulphate | HNO₃ → nitrate

concepts.example: CuSO₄ = copper sulphate.
concepts.common_confusion: Use -ate for acids with -ic (sulphuric → sulphate).

concepts.name: Salts from different acids
concepts.simple_answer: Same metal gives different salts with different acids: Zn + HCl → ZnCl₂; Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄.
concepts.example: Acid anion determines salt type.
concepts.common_confusion: Exam: write two salts of zinc with two acids.

concepts.name: Exam — salts introduction
concepts.simple_answer: Define salt → formation from neutralisation → name three salts with equations → family from HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃.
concepts.example: NaCl, ZnSO₄, CuSO₄ as examples.
concepts.common_confusion: Include balanced equations.

concepts.name: pH of salt solutions — overview
concepts.simple_answer: Salt solutions can be neutral, acidic, or basic depending on strength of acid and base that formed them.

visual.formula: Strong acid + Strong base → Neutral salt

concepts.example: NaCl solution pH 7.
concepts.remember: Parent acid and base strength matters.
concepts.common_confusion: Not all salts are neutral.

concepts.name: Strong acid + strong base salt
concepts.simple_answer: Salts from strong acid and strong base are neutral — pH 7 — e.g. NaCl, KNO₃.
concepts.example: NaCl aqueous — no excess H⁺ or OH⁻.
concepts.common_confusion: K₂SO₄ from H₂SO₄ + KOH also neutral.

concepts.name: Strong acid + weak base salt
concepts.simple_answer: Salts from strong acid and weak base are acidic — pH below 7 — e.g. NH₄Cl.
concepts.example: NH₄Cl solution turns blue litmus red slightly.
concepts.remember: NH₄⁺ ion causes acidity in water.
concepts.common_confusion: Ammonium salts are acidic.

concepts.name: Weak acid + strong base salt
concepts.simple_answer: Salts from weak acid and strong base are basic — pH above 7 — e.g. CH₃COONa.
concepts.example: Sodium acetate — basic solution.
concepts.remember: CH₃COO⁻ ion causes basicity in water.
concepts.common_confusion: Acetate salts are basic.

concepts.name: Weak acid + weak base salt
concepts.simple_answer: Salts from weak acid and weak base — pH depends on relative strength — near 7 often.
concepts.example: Ammonium acetate — approximately neutral.
concepts.common_confusion: Less emphasis in Class 10 exams.

concepts.name: Testing salt solution pH
concepts.simple_answer: Use universal indicator or pH paper on salt solution — compare to pH 7 reference.
concepts.example: NaCl green (7); NH₄Cl orange-red (<7).
concepts.common_confusion: Must dissolve salt in water first.

concepts.name: Sodium chloride — neutral
concepts.simple_answer: NaCl from HCl + NaOH — strong acid + strong base — aqueous solution pH 7.
concepts.example: Table salt solution neither acidic nor basic.
concepts.common_confusion: Ions Na⁺ and Cl⁻ do not affect pH.

concepts.name: Ammonium chloride — acidic
concepts.simple_answer: NH₄Cl from HCl + NH₄OH — strong acid + weak base — solution pH below 7.
concepts.example: Used in cough medicine and batteries.
concepts.remember: NH₄⁺ from weak base parent causes acidity.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not confuse with NH₄OH which is base.

concepts.name: Sodium carbonate — basic
concepts.simple_answer: Na₂CO₃ (washing soda) — basic salt — pH above 7; used for cleaning.
concepts.why: Common basic salt — from weak acid CO₂/H₂CO₃.
concepts.example: Washing soda cleans grease in basic medium.
concepts.remember: Carbonate ion CO₃²⁻ makes solution basic.
concepts.common_confusion: Na₂CO₃ not from single neutralisation — from NaOH + CO₂.

concepts.name: Exam — pH of salts
concepts.simple_answer: Four combinations table: strong+strong neutral, strong acid+weak base acidic, weak acid+strong base basic; give examples.
concepts.example: NaCl, NH₄Cl, CH₃COONa as three examples.
concepts.remember: Memorise four combinations + one example each.
concepts.common_confusion: Parent weakness determines salt pH.

concepts.name: Common salt NaCl — industry source
concepts.simple_answer: NaCl (common salt) is raw material for chlor-alkali industry — produces NaOH, Cl₂, H₂.
concepts.example: Brine electrolysis in factories.
concepts.common_confusion: Electrolysis of aqueous NaCl (brine).

concepts.name: Sodium hydroxide from chlor-alkali
concepts.simple_answer: NaOH (caustic soda) from chlor-alkali — used in soap, paper, textiles, and drain cleaners.
concepts.example: White pellets absorb moisture from air.
concepts.common_confusion: Handle with care — corrosive.

concepts.name: Chlorine from chlor-alkali
concepts.simple_answer: Cl₂ from chlor-alkali — used in water purification, PVC, bleaches, and disinfectants.
concepts.example: Municipal water chlorination kills bacteria.
concepts.common_confusion: Never mix bleach with acid — toxic Cl₂.

concepts.name: Hydrogen from chlor-alkali
concepts.simple_answer: H₂ from chlor-alkali — used as fuel, in margarine hardening, and ammonia manufacture.
concepts.example: H₂ collected at cathode during electrolysis.
concepts.common_confusion: Pop test applies to this H₂ too.

concepts.name: Bleaching powder Ca(OCl)₂
concepts.simple_answer: Bleaching powder calcium oxychloride Ca(OCl)₂ — from Cl₂ + slaked lime; bleaches cotton and disinfects water.
concepts.example: Used to bleach cotton in textile industry.
concepts.common_confusion: Store away from acids — releases Cl₂.

concepts.name: Baking soda NaHCO₃
concepts.simple_answer: Sodium hydrogencarbonate NaHCO₃ — baking soda; reacts with acid to release CO₂; antacid; fire extinguisher.
concepts.example: Cakes rise from CO₂ in oven heat + acid.
concepts.common_confusion: Heating alone also decomposes: NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.

concepts.name: Washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O
concepts.simple_answer: Sodium carbonate decahydrate Na₂CO₃·10H₂O — washing soda; cleaning agent; removes hardness.
concepts.why: Links to Day 16 water of crystallisation.
concepts.example: Cleans greasy clothes in basic solution.
concepts.common_confusion: Anhydrous Na₂CO₃ vs decahydrate — 10 H₂O.

concepts.name: Plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O
concepts.simple_answer: Calcium sulphate hemihydrate CaSO₄·½H₂O — plaster of Paris; sets with water to gypsum.
concepts.example: Broken bone cast hardens as gypsum.
concepts.remember: Heat gypsum to get plaster of Paris.
concepts.common_confusion: Setting is hydration back to gypsum.

concepts.name: Gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O
concepts.simple_answer: Gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O — calcium sulphate dihydrate; heated to make plaster of Paris.
concepts.example: Gypsum board in buildings.
concepts.remember: Dihydrate form stable at room temperature.
concepts.common_confusion: POP + water → gypsum (setting reaction).

concepts.name: Exam — chemicals from common salt
concepts.simple_answer: Chlor-alkali products (NaOH, Cl₂, H₂) + bleaching powder + baking soda + washing soda + gypsum/POP with uses.
concepts.example: List each chemical + one use minimum.
concepts.common_confusion: Include equations where asked.

days.title: Water of Crystallisation and Dry Crystals

concepts.name: Water of crystallisation definition
concepts.simple_answer: Fixed number of water molecules attached in crystal structure of some salts — e.g. CuSO₄·5H₂O.
concepts.example: Water part of crystal lattice.
concepts.remember: Dot formula shows water of crystallisation.
concepts.common_confusion: Different from wet salt — water is chemically bound.

concepts.name: Copper sulphate pentahydrate
concepts.simple_answer: CuSO₄·5H₂O — blue vitriol — blue crystals due to water of crystallisation.
concepts.example: Blue crystals in lab reagent bottle.
concepts.common_confusion: Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white — not blue.

concepts.name: Heating blue copper sulphate
concepts.simple_answer: Heat CuSO₄·5H₂O → white anhydrous CuSO₄ + water droplets on cool tube wall.
concepts.example: Colour change blue → white on heating.
concepts.common_confusion: Reversible — add water, turns blue again.

concepts.name: Anhydrous copper sulphate test for water
concepts.simple_answer: White anhydrous CuSO₄ turns blue on adding water — used to test for presence of water.
concepts.example: Drop water on white powder — turns blue.
concepts.common_confusion: Used as desiccant to absorb water vapour.

concepts.name: Dry crystals vs hydrated crystals
concepts.simple_answer: Dry crystals may still contain water of crystallisation — 'dry' means no free liquid water on surface.
concepts.example: Blue CuSO₄ crystals feel dry but contain 5H₂O.
concepts.remember: Water of crystallisation is inside crystal.
concepts.common_confusion: Anhydrous = no water in formula at all.

concepts.name: Glauber's salt Na₂SO₄·10H₂O
concepts.simple_answer: Sodium sulphate decahydrate Na₂SO₄·10H₂O — loses water on heating; used in medicine historically.
concepts.example: Large transparent crystals.
concepts.common_confusion: Related to washing soda hydrate.

concepts.name: Washing soda and water of crystallisation
concepts.simple_answer: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O — washing soda — 10 water molecules; effloresces in dry air.
concepts.example: Powdery white when water lost to air.
concepts.common_confusion: Anhydrous Na₂CO₃ more soluble handling in industry.

concepts.name: Efflorescence
concepts.simple_answer: Some hydrated salts lose water of crystallisation on exposure to dry air — powdery surface forms.
concepts.example: Washing soda left open becomes powdery.
concepts.common_confusion: Opposite of hygroscopic (absorbs water).

concepts.name: Gypsum and plaster water of crystallisation
concepts.simple_answer: Gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O has 2 H₂O; plaster CaSO₄·½H₂O has half H₂O — interconvert on heat/hydrate.
concepts.example: POP sets by rejoining water as gypsum.
concepts.common_confusion: Heating gypsum drives off 1.5 H₂O to make POP.

concepts.name: Unit 2 complete
concepts.simple_answer: Unit 2 Acids, Bases and Salts complete — all 160 cards; proceed to Practice when unlocked.
concepts.example: 200 MCQs in bank when available.
concepts.common_confusion: Review pH, neutralisation, and industrial chemicals.
